First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,.
$$

Differentiating $y(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x})+{z}^{-1} & ={x}^{2}{({z}^{-1})}^{2} \\ -\frac{x}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{z} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{x}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{z} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{z}{x} & =-x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}\,z & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=-\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-x\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)dx} \\  & ={e}^{-\int 1/xdx} \\  & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|x{|}^{-1}} \\  & =|x{|}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}\,z) & =\frac{1}{x}\cdot (-x) \\ \frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}z & =-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{z}{x}] & =-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{z}{x}]\,\text{d}x & =\int -1\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z}{x} & =-x+C \\ z & =-{x}^{2}+Cx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =-{x}^{2}+Cx \\ y & =\frac{1}{Cx-{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
